title: What is the biggest AI game dev problem?
author: gcampos
selftext:
I really like how AI was able to make easier to create assets and code, but one thing that I was wondering is what problems, in spite all the AI advances (or because of it), are still big pain points and unresolved for game devs using AI.

For me in particular is how easy is to tell if an asset is AI generated, but its really hard something to tell \*why\* looks AI generated.

comments.author: Unique-Watercress225
comments.body: yes. i think this is the same problem with webdesign, gamedev. and so on

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body: Idk, for webdesign I can more easily tell why looks like AI generated (neon colors, over use of accent colors, round rectangles with shade on one side, over done gradients, llm troped text, etc...)

comments.author: ScrumptiousChildren
comments.body:
How is that a problem? That’s just a feature of how AI generates stuff.

A large, real problem that I see is that AI slop really drags the reputation of AI into the dirt. People are generally more against games made with AI assistance than they would be if crappy AI products weren’t so abundant.

replies.author: cxfoulke
replies.body: gamers have no morals if the game is good they will accept anything from warcrime commiting developers to gacha 0.01% drop rates. If people are rejecting Ai games its because it sticks out and brings the quality of the game down. Folks simply need to do better.

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body:
I think it is, knowing exactly what is wrong is how you can fix it. For code that is not a problem because when I see something wrong with the code, I know exactly why its wrong, that is not the same for art (at least for myself).

I agree with the reputation thing, that is not very different from Unity3d games from 10 years ago

comments.author: No-Marionberry-772
comments.body:
I think the biggest problem is first game design.
Ive been building games as a hobby for a long time but I was never great at getting things done.  Now that I can prototype ideas quickly, I'm quickly learning that while I believe I understand what makes games fun for me, I'm not sure how to design those things from scratch.

Second on the list is sound design and integration, which may impact my first.  Good sound design can literally make all the difference between an exciting experience and a boring one.  some genres make this more important than others, but its important in most regardless.

replies.author: Designer-Stay7977
replies.body: Yeah this is a big one I feel like. It makes you kind of realize exactly why studios have balancing teams and such, however I do think the AI can tremendously help with a lot of that. Also not even the big AAA studios get it right either and often have to patch things and such later, so as long as the game itself is fun I think it's not too tragic.

replies.author: nokafein
replies.body:
ai can't help for designing a game. game is essentially a multidisipliner art. ai can't do art. anything ai touches is destined for the average of everything that has been produced before it. game design requires constant creative solutions for novel problems. And no problem are same. because each game are different. 

all the aaa studios are targeting that average to appeal masses. never compare yourself to aaa when it comes to anything. because they have lots of money and they are trying to turn their lots of money to even more lots of money. you don't have that money. your only chance is to find your "gimmick". and i can't find it for you. if you don't know every single details about how your system works, that system is destined to fail. if you don't know how something behaves, you can't make it fun or engaging. ai can help you polish and iterate that system but it can't provide anything with creative value.

replies.author: Trashy_io
replies.body: yeah game design and balance as well as just overall creative thinking AI does not really excel unless you're trying to make a clone

replies.author: No-Marionberry-772
replies.body:
I think you may be going a little extreme, but its definitely not something that ai does easily.
Like, I haven't dont anything I think is great yet, and so some of this could be wishful thinking.

I think you
 really have to break down your idea, define major groups, identify the loops, figure out opportunity costs, and really build out a comprehensive game design, which is a lot of information that has to be coordinated and validated against itself.  the scale isn't something ai handles well, and there isn't a computational solution to it afaik, so you have to really go over it yourself.

comments.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
comments.body:
Here is what I think looks ai generated even though people have trouble saying why; I think it has to do with non-artists or beginner artist generating assets then when they put them together they clash. I see things like super detailed backgrounds then fairly detailed characters with poor animations and the whole thing just visually falls apart. 

Im going with pretty simple pixel art with stuff I could make manually or almost make manually (and sometimes I just make it the old fashioned way. I’ve generated some really cool detailed art but if I can’t make all art consistent with the really pretty stuff it just makes the non pretty stuff, for pretty but in a different way stuff stand out. 

In short, I think to ai gen art successfully you need an artist’s eye and that just takes practice.

replies.author: jpeggdev
replies.body: I’ve had good luck with Claude Code taking an asset and telling it to keep the mood and palette the same.

replies.author: pspahn
replies.body: Design wise, it's the fonts that stick out to me. Often undersized and with poor contrast and difficult to read.

comments.author: MeridianCastaway
comments.body: That game design and game development is not the same, and game design is what makes a game a stayer in the end past novelty

comments.author: PykeTheTitan
comments.body:
People keep saying game design, but that is very much a developer problem and not an ai problem, it is just a tool

imo what I have found ai to struggle with is the art side. I think a good developer can use ai to efficiently implement good game design but 3d modeling and animation capabilities are not up to par quite yet

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
>\*why\* looks AI generated.

That is because it averages, it makes the most generic version of anything. Go wild for better results. Like either use an wild example, or tell it to use an style that you don't think looks AI.

  
My problem is with paid AI, they often have like an "project" option that allows the AI to forget, but it is limited. - Using AI is like firing an arrow, like playing an game of marble, navigating an maze. Resetting when you failed makes it easier to eventually suceed.

With custom models you just reset, but AI companies are so greedy for info that they don't want users to just reset all the time.

comments.author: Motor-Master-4545
comments.body: 3D generation with perfect lowpoly retopology.

comments.author: Designer-Stay7977
comments.body: Right now I feel like my biggest problem is not having people being able to test your game to see if the concept is really that fun or what needs to be changed based on actual player feedback. It's especially scary because it's so easy for people to go "cool game concept, YOINK" too unless you've already put a great amount of effort into it as well. 😭

replies.author: Orlandogameschool
replies.body:
You want to make a prompt that acts as a game tester and audits your game

. I have an idle game I made and did that. 

It played the game by itself and came  back with a  report  like hey I  made it to mission 8  then died. Missions 1-3 are way too easy let’s scale back on resources  and make the following adjustments….this helped a lot

replies.author: Designer-Stay7977
replies.body: That's a really smart idea, I like that! Thank you.

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body:
That is a real issue! Its incredible hard to get constant high quality feedback, either the feedback is too sparse, too superficial or too nice.

I honestly don't give my feedback for people online because idk how the person would react, most people don't take feedback as well as they think they do

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
In general?  Code is now very accessible but most people making games have no eye for design whatsoever.  They're just making crude copy/pastes of games they like or think will be profitable.

  
For someone with design talent the blocker is still creative - sprites, music, animations, 3d models, etc.  The one click "make pretty assets" stuff isn't anywhere near production quality

comments.author: DuckAndQwack
comments.body: Costs of the AI.

comments.author: jpeggdev
comments.body: Getting people to accept the use of AI in creating the game at all. I can’t remember which games or maybe multiple that I’ve seen where they released it and it did pretty good and then it comes out that AI was used and they lose a good chunk of players. You mainly see the pushback against it for generating assets, but sometimes for the programming as well. What is so different between using AI to write a library vs downloading one written by hand? I can’t remember which understand for security related stuff but we also freely download them too from NPM all the time and we’ve seen how malware hasn’t gotten into some of the more mature library packages in the last few years.

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body: I think it will be a matter of time for this to become a non issue, already everyone uses AI these days, I can't image a world where development goes back to what it was.

replies.author: jpeggdev

comments.author: AliveAndNotForgotten

comments.author: Dan_Fury
comments.body: The biggest pain point is memory and context. I am currently in the final phase of a bigger unreal game entirely coded with Claude and every bug I fix introduces a bunch of new ones because the AI can't remember what it did a few weeks ago and why it did it. It's super shit going constantly in circles and fixing the same bugs for the xth time.

replies.author: gcampos
replies.body:
Do you have automated tests?

That works well for regular development to prevent the problem you are having, but im not sure how easy is to write unit tests and automations with Unreal

replies.author: Dan_Fury
replies.body: I do have a few that Claude manages itself and without them it would be ten times worse. I bet a better programmer could add more to reduce these outbreaks, but that's why I use Claude in the first place, I suck at programming. I also build a benchmark and a visual audit I run once a week to catch all these errors as early as I can. It's still super frustrating because AI can e.g. screw up a graphic by replacing a sound file. That actually happened yesterday. Another example, yesterday we had a shader bug that happened mostly because of how TSR handled this particular shader. TAA didn't do that so Claude wanted to switch the whole project and destroy all low end compatibility because it "forgot" that TAA cannot do screen percentage scaling. It explicitly explained the limitations and just forgot about our Steam Deck profile and low settings.

replies.author: Ahenian
replies.body: I haven't dealt with bigger vibe coded codebases, but do you ever prompt claude to refactor/consolidate/simplify/detangle/reduce your code? AI given free reign tends to overengineer features and be overly verbose, leads to bloat and stuffing your context with useless tokens and your AI getting confused by its own code. Using a different LLM to review is also very useful.

comments.author: HealthyWest6482
comments.body: the speed at which prototyping turns into implementation leaves zero room for brakes when dopamine is the gas

comments.author: Playistheway
comments.body:
The biggest AI game dev problem is that people with limited technical skills, who cannot produce the output themselves, are now unable to verify the efficacy of their solution and cannot articulate the problems in the output where they lack expertise. For example, the main reason that AI art feels wrong is that it uses a photogrammetry technique for its material painting; it needs to infer how a static image maps to geometry, and that inference carries an implicit standard of error. 

The reality that a lot of "AI game devs" don't want to face is that a game development studio would not hire an AI-assisted developer to produce code that they cannot explain to the rest of the team.

comments.author: Entropydemic
comments.body:
I love Ai, but I assume for the reason of copying assets in bulk it gives its distinct output as the amalgamation of things. Ai can generate anything, so you have to get creative in order to make it appear as if the Ai didn't do it all. Otherwise, you get a very typical, symmetrical output which we all can easily recognize. You can make sprites without ever editing a thing, or, you can just design the thing and use the Ai as a helper rather than a producer.

Secondly, is the realization that logic is essential in game coding whether you code it or not. You can't expect Ai to perfectly output logic if you don't use any yourself, and it shows. Games are coming out daily now, but how many of them will you remember, and talk about for years? Ai made or not, a solid plan is essential.

https://i.redd.it/h61elq7ap2jh1.gif

For me, the most tricky part is always graphic. Especially graphic that doesnt feel like AI generated, consistency, and animation(i gave up on this part)
